title: The Great Enemy of Truth
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Drawing on a JFK commencement address and Gerald Graff's pedagogical argument in Clueless in Academe, Stuart Jr. argues that the greatest threat to truth in the classroom is not deliberate lying but the myth — the unexamined assumption held with conviction but without reflection. JFK's formulation that students enjoy the comfort of opinion without the discomfort of thought is applied to myths Stuart identifies in both student culture and teacher culture. The piece calls for classrooms to make the discomfort of thought as regular and unavoidable as the class bell, positioning the teaching of argumentation as the discipline best suited to combating mythic thinking in both students and teachers.
points: JFK's distinction between a lie — deliberate deception — and a myth — unexamined assumption — equips teachers with language for a subtler and more pervasive threat to student thinking.
Graff's thesis that the disciplines are all cultures of argument gives teachers a unifying rationale for teaching argumentation across every subject, not just English.
Common student myths — school is pointless, grades equal learning, ability is fixed — operate precisely because they never receive the discomfort of thought that would expose their inadequacy.
Teacher myths, including fixed student labels and relationships-as-singular-lever thinking, are equally persistent and equally damaging to professional effectiveness.
Stuart identifies his own susceptibility to mythic thinking, modeling the self-awareness he recommends: the soul slips easily into the autopilot of its opinions without deliberate effort.
quotes: For the great enemy of truth is very often not the lie — deliberate, contrived and dishonest — but the myth — persistent, persuasive, and unrealistic. Too often we hold fast to the cliches of our forebears. We subject all facts to a prefabricated set of interpretations.

What all the disciplines have in common, in Graff's view, is that they are cultures of argument. If we did a better job making this clear to students — which is basically the goal of Graff and Birkenstein's popular They Say, I Say book — then our students would have a much better (more successful, more engaging) time with school.

A myth, on the other hand, is an unexamined assumption. You don't need to be convinced of what he's calling a myth; you don't even need to think about it. It's just there, persistent, persuasive, and detached from reality.
Do my students enjoy the comfort of opinion without the discomfort of thought? Do teachers? I think many of them do.

I know for myself, my soul slips very easily into the autopilot of my opinions; left to my own stubborn inclinations, I'll avoid the discomfort of thought like the best of 'em. So colleague: may our classes be places in which the discomfort of thought is as regular and unavoidable as the ringing of the bell.
